big_idea: Most conflict and disconnection comes from a habitual, judgment-based way of speaking and listening. By observing without evaluating, naming genuine feelings, connecting them to underlying needs, and making clear requests, not demands, people can communicate in a way that stays connected to compassion even in conflict.

tool.label: The four-part NVC process, OFNR
tool.text: State a concrete Observation, a fact, not a judgment, name the Feeling it brings up, identify the underlying Need or value driving that feeling, and make a specific, actionable Request, not a demand. For example: when I see or hear X, I feel Y, because I need Z; would you be willing to do W?
tool.note: Formalized by Rosenberg as the 4-Part NVC Process, taught today by the Center for Nonviolent Communication exactly as OFNR.

ideas.title: Observation vs. evaluation
ideas.text: Separate what actually happened, a fact a camera could record, from your interpretation of it; mixing the two triggers defensiveness in the listener.

ideas.title: Feelings vs. thoughts
ideas.text: True feeling words, hurt, anxious, relieved, differ from disguised judgments, like feeling ignored or attacked, which are actually interpretations of the other person's behavior.

ideas.title: Underlying needs
ideas.text: Every feeling points to a met or unmet universal human need, connection, autonomy, safety; naming the need, not the other person's fault, is the path to resolution.

ideas.title: Requests vs. demands
ideas.text: A request stays a request only if you can accept no gracefully; if refusal brings punishment or guilt-tripping, it was really a demand.

ideas.title: Jackal vs. giraffe language
ideas.text: Rosenberg used jackal to represent judgmental, blaming speech and giraffe to represent compassionate NVC-style speech, as a teaching metaphor.

ideas.title: Self-empathy and anger
ideas.text: Anger is treated as a signal of an unmet need rather than something to suppress or vent destructively; process it by identifying the need beneath it before speaking.

try_it: Rewrite one recent complaint using OFNR: state the observable fact, your feeling, your need, and a concrete request, before you say it out loud.
Catch yourself using a judgment word this week and translate it into an observation plus a feeling instead.
Practice empathic listening once: when someone vents to you, reflect back their feelings and needs instead of offering advice or defending yourself.
Next time you're angry, pause and ask what need of mine isn't being met right now before responding.
best_for: People wanting to reduce blame and defensiveness in close relationships
Therapists, mediators, parents, and communication-skills learners
less_useful: Readers in acute, high-stakes adversarial negotiations needing fast tactics
Those who find the required language patterns stilted or slow-going at first

related.why: A complementary framework for the same feelings-and-identity layer of hard conversations
A modern, research-driven companion on matching your listening to what a conversation needs
